\chapter{Directed Graphs}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Directed Graphs}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.DirectedGraphs.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$]
\lean{edgeConnectivity}
\label{edgeConnectivity}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCut}
The least number of edges one must cut to break $G$ apart.  "$G$ is
$k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G} throughout this file --- see
\texttt{robbins\_orientation} ($k = 2$) and \texttt{exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian}.

Mathlib has no edge-connectivity, so this is the repo's notion
restated locally.  \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} in $\mathbb{N}$ reproduces the book's trivial-graph
convention automatically --- but it also means a graph with \emph{no} edge cut (a
one-vertex graph) gets $\kappa' = 0$, which is the source of the \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} gap in
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The bridge \texttt{Digraph $\to$ Quiver}: \texttt{Quiver.\{0\} V} has \texttt{Hom : V $\to$ V $\to$ Prop},\dots]
\lean{Digraph.toQuiver}
\label{Digraph.toQuiver}
\leanok
A quiver is a vertex set together with, for each ordered pair, a
\emph{type} of arrows.  Taking that type to be a \texttt{Prop} --- arrow or no arrow --- recovers
exactly a digraph, and Mathlib's \texttt{Quiver.Path} then supplies directed walks for
free, which \texttt{Digraph} (a bare \texttt{Adj} with a lattice API) does not.

\textbf{!} Deliberately \textbf{not} an \texttt{instance}.  The chapter routinely
handles several digraphs on one vertex type at once --- $D$ and its converse $\breve{D}$,
$D$ and a reorientation of one arc (exercise 10.2.1) --- and a global instance would
make \texttt{Quiver.Path} ambiguous between them.  The cost is that every use site must
write \texttt{@Quiver.Path V D.toQuiver u v} explicitly, which is why the statements below
are visually heavy.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A directed path: a \texttt{Quiver.Path} with no repeated vertex]
\lean{Digraph.IsDirectedPath}
\label{Digraph.IsDirectedPath}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Follow the arrows, never against them; a directed path additionally
never revisits a vertex.  The book stresses (figure 10.3) that there is *no close
relationship between the lengths of paths and directed paths in a digraph* --- the
digraph there has arbitrarily long paths but no directed path of length above one.
Theorem 10.1 is remarkable precisely because it recovers control of directed-path
length from the chromatic number.

\textbf{!} \texttt{Quiver.Path} \textbf{is} the directed walk, so a directed path is
a \texttt{Quiver.Path} with \texttt{Nodup} vertices.  Note the book's directed walks are
\emph{non-null}, whereas \texttt{Quiver.Path.nil} is available here; that mismatch is harmless
for paths but bites for Euler tours (see \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour}).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A directed cycle: a positive-length closed walk whose vertices (bar the repeated endpoint) are distinct]
\lean{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle}
\label{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Follow the arrows all the way round and return to where you started,
never repeating a vertex en route.  Directed cycles are the subject of \S{}10.3: Moon
(theorem 10.3) finds them of every length in a diconnected tournament, and
Ghouila-Houri (theorem 10.4) finds a spanning one under a degree condition.

\texttt{0 < length} excludes \texttt{nil}; \texttt{vertices.tail.Nodup} allows the
repeated basepoint at the two ends while forbidding any other repeat.  Note a
\textbf{loop} \texttt{D.Adj v v} counts as a directed cycle of length $1$ under this
definition, which is what makes the acyclicity hypotheses below (\texttt{hacyc})
automatically exclude loops --- relied on by \texttt{exists\_topological\_ordering}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$v$ is reachable from $u$]
\lean{Digraph.Reachable}
\label{Digraph.Reachable}
\leanok
You can get from $u$ to $v$ travelling only along arrows in their
given direction.  Reachability is \emph{not} symmetric --- that asymmetry is the whole
point of directing a graph, and is what makes diconnection a strictly stronger
condition than connection.

\texttt{Relation.ReflTransGen D.Adj} rather than an existential over
\texttt{Quiver.Path}.  The two agree (a path witnesses reachability and conversely), but
\texttt{ReflTransGen} comes with induction principles and is \emph{reflexive}, matching the
book's convention that every vertex reaches itself.  Being defined directly from
\texttt{Adj}, it needs no \texttt{Quiver} instance, so $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} coexist freely ---
which \texttt{converse\_reachable} relies on.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$ is diconnected: every vertex reaches every other]
\lean{Digraph.Diconnected}
\label{Digraph.Diconnected}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Reachable}
Wherever you start and wherever you want to go, some route respecting
the arrows exists.  In the road-network reading of \S{}10.6 this is exactly the
condition that a one-way system lets traffic flow freely --- every junction remains
reachable from every other, and Robbins' theorem 10.5 says $2$-edge-connectivity is
precisely what makes it achievable.

Stated directly as "every ordered pair is reachable" rather
than via dicomponents, which avoids constructing the quotient.  The two agree: one
dicomponent means the equivalence relation is total.  Note this is \emph{not} symmetric
by fiat --- \texttt{$\forall$ u v, Reachable u v} quantifies over ordered pairs, so both directions
are demanded.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$d^{-}(v)$, the indegree]
\lean{Digraph.indegree}
\label{Digraph.indegree}
\leanok
How many arrows point \emph{into} $v$.  Exercise 10.1.2 gives the directed
handshake lemma $\sum d^{-}(v) = \varepsilon = \sum d^{+}(v)$ --- each arc is counted once by its head and
once by its tail, which is why the directed sum is $\varepsilon$ and not $2\varepsilon$.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits).  Counts \emph{vertices} $u$ with
\texttt{D.Adj u v}, not arcs --- the same thing here, since \texttt{Digraph} is a bare relation and
admits no parallel arcs.  Needs \texttt{[DecidableRel D.Adj]} for the \texttt{filter}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$d^{+}(v)$, the outdegree]
\lean{Digraph.outdegree}
\label{Digraph.outdegree}
\leanok
How many arrows point \emph{out of} $v$.  Together with the indegree this
refines the single degree of an undirected graph into two numbers, and their
interplay drives most of the chapter: Euler tours need them equal (exercise
10.3.2), Ghouila-Houri's theorem 10.4 needs both large, and exercise 10.1.10 asks
for an orientation making them nearly equal everywhere.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  The exact mirror of \texttt{indegree} under
\texttt{converse}, which is the content of exercise 10.1.5(a)(ii).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$, the number of arcs]
\lean{Digraph.arcCount}
\label{Digraph.arcCount}
\leanok
Count the ordered pairs $(u, v)$ for which an arc runs from $u$ to
$v$.  This is the $\varepsilon$ of exercise 10.1.2's handshake lemma and of exercise 10.1.1's
$2^\varepsilon$ orientation count.

Since \texttt{Digraph} allows no parallel arcs in the same direction,
$\varepsilon$ is simply the size of the adjacency relation, counted as a \texttt{Finset (V $\times$ V)}.
Note this differs from the book for multi-digraphs, which B\&M permit --- a point that
also forces the restatement of \texttt{adjMatrix} below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\delta^{-}$, the minimum indegree]
\lean{Digraph.minIndegree}
\label{Digraph.minIndegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.indegree}
The least number of arrows pointing into any one vertex.  Exercise
10.1.3(a) says an acyclic digraph must have $\delta^{-} = 0$, which is what makes
topological ordering possible; exercises 10.1.6--10.1.7 turn a large $\delta^{-}$ into long
directed paths and cycles.

\textbf{!} $\bigsqcap$ over $\mathbb{N}$ is \texttt{Nat.sInf}, and \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, so on an
empty carrier this silently returns $0$ rather than being undefined.  Every use
site below carries \texttt{[Nonempty V]} for that reason.  Only the \emph{minima} are defined
here; $\Delta^{-}$, $\Delta^{+}$ are never needed by a surviving statement.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\delta^{+}$, the minimum outdegree]
\lean{Digraph.minOutdegree}
\label{Digraph.minOutdegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.outdegree}
The least number of arrows leaving any one vertex.  By the converse
symmetry of exercise 10.1.5, statements about $\delta^{-}$ transfer to $\delta^{+}$ and back ---
exactly how exercise 10.1.5(b) deduces $\delta^{+} = 0$ for acyclic digraphs from
$\delta^{-} = 0$, without repeating the argument.

Same \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} caveat as \texttt{minIndegree}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The converse $\breve{D}$: reverse every arc]
\lean{Digraph.converse}
\label{Digraph.converse}
\leanok
Turn every arrow around.  It is an involution ($\breve{\breve{D}} = D$), it swaps
indegree with outdegree, and it reverses reachability --- so every theorem about
digraphs comes with a free dual, obtained by applying it to the converse.  Exercise
10.1.5(a) records exactly these three facts and (b) puts them to work.

A one-line \texttt{Digraph.mk} with the arguments of \texttt{Adj} swapped, so
\texttt{converse\_converse} should be \texttt{rfl}-adjacent.  Because \texttt{Reachable} is defined from
\texttt{Adj} and not through a \texttt{Quiver} instance, $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} can appear in the
same statement without ambiguity --- see \texttt{converse\_reachable}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$ is strict: loopless (\texttt{Digraph} already forbids parallel same-direction arcs)]
\lean{Digraph.IsStrict}
\label{Digraph.IsStrict}
\leanok
The directed analogue of "simple".  Note a strict digraph \emph{may} have
both $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$ --- forbidding that is what makes an orientation, which is a
strictly stronger condition.  Strictness is the standing hypothesis of exercises
10.1.6, 10.1.7 and theorem 10.4, where it guarantees that $\delta^{+}$ out-neighbours are
$\delta^{+}$ genuinely \emph{distinct} vertices.

Since \texttt{Digraph} is a bare relation it already forbids repeated
arcs in the same direction, so the book's second clause is automatic and strictness
reduces to looplessness --- \texttt{Irreflexive D.Adj}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$ is an orientation of $G$ --- the chapter's keystone gap]
\lean{Digraph.IsOrientationOf}
\label{Digraph.IsOrientationOf}
\leanok
Make every edge one-way, choosing a direction for each.  Orientations
are the chapter's central object: exercise 10.1.1 counts them ($2^\varepsilon$), the remark
after theorem 10.1 builds one whose directed paths are short, exercise 10.1.10 one
that is degree-balanced, and \S{}10.6 asks which graphs admit \emph{diconnected} ones ---
Robbins' theorem 10.5.

Two clauses.  The first, \texttt{D.toSimpleGraphInclusive = G}, says
the underlying graph comes back out as $G$.  The second,
\texttt{$\forall$ u v, $\lnot$(D.Adj u v $\land$ D.Adj v u)}, forbids making an edge two-way --- without it the
associated digraph $D(G)$ would count as an orientation of $G$, which it is not.
Taking $u = v$ in the second clause also forces looplessness, so an orientation is
automatically strict.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$ is a tournament: an orientation of the complete graph]
\lean{Digraph.IsTournament}
\label{Digraph.IsTournament}
\leanok
Every pair of players meets exactly once and the arrow points from
winner to loser.  Tournaments are remarkably well behaved: every one has a directed
Hamilton path (R\'edei, corollary 10.1) and a "king" reaching everyone in at most two
steps (corollary 10.2); diconnected ones are vertex-pancyclic (Moon, theorem 10.3)
and hence have directed Hamilton cycles (Camion).  \S{}10.7 uses them to rank players.

Unfolded rather than defined as "\texttt{IsOrientationOf} some
complete graph": \texttt{Irreflexive D.Adj} plus, for distinct $u$, $v$, exactly one of
\texttt{D.Adj u v}, \texttt{D.Adj v u}.  The $\leftrightarrow \lnot$ phrasing packs both "at least one" (from
completeness of the underlying graph) and "at most one" (from being an orientation)
into a single clause.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[B\&M's $(S, T)$: arcs with tail in $S$, head in $T$]
\lean{Digraph.arcsBetween}
\label{Digraph.arcsBetween}
\leanok
The arcs crossing from $S$ into $T$, counted with their direction.
Unlike the undirected edge cut $[S, \bar{S}]$, the directed version splits into two
generally \emph{unequal} halves $(S, \bar{S})$ and $(\bar{S}, S)$ --- which is precisely what
$k$-arc-connectivity measures, and what theorem 10.6 has to balance.

A \texttt{Finset (V $\times$ V)} obtained by filtering the product $S \times^{s} T$,
so $|(S, T)|$ is its \texttt{card}.  Used in \texttt{IsKArcConnected} and in Moon's theorem 10.3,
where the book's "$(S, T)$ must be nonempty" becomes a cardinality claim.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$ is $k$-arc-connected: every nonempty proper cut has $\ge k$ outgoing arcs]
\lean{Digraph.IsKArcConnected}
\label{Digraph.IsKArcConnected}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.arcsBetween}
However you split the vertices in two, at least $k$ arrows point from
the first part to the second.  Exercise 10.3.5 says $1$-arc-connected is the same
as diconnected, and exercise 10.3.6(b) that $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when
$G$ is $k$-edge-connected.  Nash-Williams' theorem --- of which theorem 10.6 is the
easy special case --- says every $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected
orientation.

\textbf{!} The book says \textbf{nontrivial} digraph, and this definition
drops that.  On a one-vertex carrier there is no nonempty proper $S$, so the
condition is vacuously true for \emph{every} $k$ --- which is why statements consuming it
must supply \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} themselves.  \texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one}
does; \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} does not, and is false in consequence
(see its docstring).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The induced subdigraph on $S$ (kept on the same carrier to avoid subtype juggling)]
\lean{Digraph.induce}
\label{Digraph.induce}
\leanok
Keep only the vertices in $S$ and the arcs with both ends there.  The
dicomponents of $D$ are the induced subdigraphs $D[V_{i}]$ on the diconnection classes,
and theorem 10.2's induction removes ${v} \cup N^{+}(v)$ this way.

Kept on the \textbf{same carrier} $V$, with membership in $S$ folded
into \texttt{Adj}, rather than moving to a subtype.  This avoids subtype juggling across
the many statements that induce, at the cost that \texttt{induce D S} has isolated
vertices outside $S$ --- harmless, since every consumer only asks about arcs.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The list of arcs traversed by a directed walk]
\lean{Digraph.arcsOf}
\label{Digraph.arcsOf}
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Reading off the arrows a directed walk uses, in order.  This is what a
\emph{trail} condition quantifies over --- a directed trail repeats no arc --- and what a
directed Euler tour must exhaust.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this definition has a \texttt{sorry} body.}  It is declared
\texttt{List (V $\times$ V) := sorry}, so \texttt{arcsOf} is an \emph{opaque, unspecified} function, not the
arc list of anything.  This is the most damaging defect in the file, because the
opacity propagates:
\item \texttt{IsDirectedTrail} and \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour} are defined from it, so both are
  meaningless as stated;
\item and therefore \texttt{exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff} (exercise 10.3.2),
  \texttt{deBruijnDigraph\_exists\_directedEulerTour} and \texttt{exists\_arcDisjoint\_directedPaths}
  (exercise 10.3.3) say nothing --- which is the entire \S{}10.5 computer-drum
  application plus the flow precursor to chapter 11.
\emph{ It also violates the project convention (\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): }never \texttt{sorry} in
  a \texttt{def}* --- a \texttt{sorry}-ed proof is an honest debt, a \texttt{sorry}-ed definition is a
  silent change of meaning.

\emph{The repair} is a routine structural recursion on \texttt{Quiver.Path}, whose two
constructors are \texttt{nil : Path a a} and \texttt{cons : Path a b $\to$ (b ⟶ c) $\to$ Path a c}:

    arcsOf nil        = []
    arcsOf (cons p e) = arcsOf p ++ [(b, c)]

with $b$, $c$ the source and target of the arrow $e$.  Nothing about it is
delicate; the outline simply left it unspecified.  This is a change of \emph{meaning},
not of annotation, so it has been flagged rather than made here.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A directed trail: no repeated arc]
\lean{Digraph.IsDirectedTrail}
\label{Digraph.IsDirectedTrail}
\uses{Digraph.arcsOf, Digraph.toQuiver}
Follow the arrows, never using the same arrow twice, though you may
revisit vertices.  The directed analogue of \S{}1.6's trail, and the notion an Euler
tour refines.

\textbf{!} Inherits the \texttt{arcsOf} defect: since \texttt{arcsOf} is \texttt{sorry}, this
predicate is \texttt{(opaque list).Nodup} and means nothing.  Repairing \texttt{arcsOf} repairs
this automatically.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A directed Euler tour: a closed directed trail using every arc]
\lean{Digraph.IsDirectedEulerTour}
\label{Digraph.IsDirectedEulerTour}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedTrail, Digraph.arcsOf, Digraph.toQuiver}
The directed version of Euler's problem --- traverse every one-way
street exactly once and return to the start.  Exercise 10.3.2 gives the criterion:
possible exactly when $D$ is connected and $d^{+}(v) = d^{-}(v)$ everywhere, the directed
analogue of theorem 4.1's even-degree condition, because every visit uses one arrow
in and one out.  \S{}10.5 uses it to design an efficient computer drum via the de
Bruijn digraph.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective on two counts.}
1. \emph{Inherits the \texttt{arcsOf} defect} --- both conjuncts are stated in terms of an opaque
   function, so the predicate currently means nothing.
2. \emph{Admits the null walk.}  B\&M's directed walks are explicitly \textbf{non-null}
   (\S{}10.1), so \texttt{nil} is not a directed tour for them; here \texttt{Quiver.Path.nil}
   satisfies both conjuncts vacuously (\texttt{[].Nodup}, and no arc to exhaust when $D$
   has none).  This is not cosmetic: it makes \texttt{exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff} false
   outright --- see the counterexample there.

\emph{The repair} for (2) is to add \texttt{0 < Quiver.Path.length p}, matching "non-null".
Both repairs change \emph{meaning}, so they are flagged rather than made here.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$ is unilateral: any two vertices are comparable by reachability]
\lean{Digraph.IsUnilateral}
\label{Digraph.IsUnilateral}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Reachable}
Weaker than diconnected --- you need only get \emph{one} way between any two
vertices, not both.  Exercise 10.2.2 characterises it: $D$ is unilateral exactly
when it has a spanning directed \emph{walk}.

The disjunction is over \texttt{Reachable}, which is reflexive, so the
case $u = v$ is automatic.  Note "unilateral" sits strictly between "connected"
(underlying graph) and "diconnected".
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The 0/1 adjacency matrix of $D$]
\lean{Digraph.adjMatrix}
\label{Digraph.adjMatrix}
\leanok
Record a $1$ where an arrow runs from $v_{i}$ to $v_{j}$ and $0$ otherwise.
Unlike the undirected case (\S{}1.3) this matrix is \emph{not} symmetric --- its asymmetry
encodes the orientations.  Exercise 10.1.8 shows $A^{k}$ counts directed walks of
length $k$, and \S{}10.7 uses the powers of $A$ to rank tournament players via the
level score vectors $s_{i} = A^{i}J$.

\textbf{!} Restated: \texttt{Digraph} has no arc multiplicities, so entries are
$0$ or $1$ rather than a count.  For strict digraphs --- which every \S{}10.7 statement
is about, tournaments being orientations --- the two agree, so nothing is lost where
it is used.  The value type $\alpha$ is left generic so the same matrix serves the
$\mathbb{N}$-valued counting of exercise 10.1.8 and any later numeric work.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The condensation $\hat{D}$: dicomponents contracted]
\lean{Digraph.condensation}
\label{Digraph.condensation}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Shrink each dicomponent to a single point and keep the arcs between
them.  Exercise 10.1.9 shows the condensation is \emph{acyclic} --- a directed cycle among
dicomponents would merge them into one --- so by exercise 10.1.3(b) the dicomponents
can be topologically ordered, which is what \S{}10.7 uses to rank the participants of a
non-diconnected tournament, and what exercise 10.2.1 uses on tournaments.

\textbf{!} The $a \ne b$ clause is a \textbf{recorded correction}, not a
transcription.  Taken literally the book's condition puts an arc from $w_{i}$ to $w_{i}$
whenever $D_{i}$ has any internal arc --- a loop at every non-trivial dicomponent --- which
would make \texttt{condensation\_acyclic} false, since a loop is a directed cycle of length
$1$.  B\&M plainly intend $i \ne j$.

The vertex type is \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}, Mathlib's quotient by mutual
reachability, which is exactly the set of dicomponents.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[dirDist]
\lean{Digraph.dirDist}
\label{Digraph.dirDist}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
$\vec{d}(u,v)$. \textbf{!} \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} when $v$ is unreachable from $u$.

The fewest arrows you must follow to get from $u$ to $v$.  Unlike the
undirected distance of \S{}1.6 this is \emph{not symmetric} --- $\vec{d}(u,v)$ and $\vec{d}(v,u)$ may
differ, which is the whole reason \S{}10.7 needs $d + 3$ rather than something
symmetric.

\textbf{!} \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, so an unreachable $v$ gets distance $0$
rather than $\infty$.  The definition is therefore faithful only on diconnected
digraphs --- which is exactly where the book defines it, and both consumers
(\texttt{tournament\_adjMatrix\_pow\_pos}, \texttt{dirDiameter}) carry \texttt{hdicon}.  Minimising over
\texttt{Quiver.Path} lengths rather than over \texttt{Reachable} witnesses, since the \emph{length} is
what is wanted.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[dirDiameter]
\lean{Digraph.dirDiameter}
\label{Digraph.dirDiameter}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.dirDist}
The worst case of the directed distance --- how far apart two vertices
can be when you must respect the arrows.  Theorem 10.7 shows that for a diconnected
tournament on at least five vertices $A^{d+3}$ is entrywise positive, where $d$ is
this diameter, and corollary 10.7 turns that into the primitivity that makes the
\S{}10.7 ranking method converge.

A \texttt{Finset.sup} over all ordered pairs, so the diagonal $\vec{d}(v,v) = 0$
is included harmlessly.  Inherits \texttt{dirDist}'s \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} caveat: on a
non-diconnected digraph the diameter is silently too small.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs. \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric,\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph}
\leanok
Make every street two-way.  This embeds undirected graph theory inside
directed graph theory: exercise 10.3.6 shows paths in $G$ correspond exactly to
directed paths in $D(G)$, and $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.  Exercise 10.3.1 uses the embedding to derive Dirac's theorem
4.3 from Ghouila-Houri's 10.4.

One line: \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric and irreflexive, so it
\emph{is} the arc relation of $D(G)$ --- the "two oppositely oriented arcs" are the two
directions of the symmetric relation.  Note $D(G)$ is emphatically \textbf{not} an
orientation of $G$ (\texttt{IsOrientationOf}'s second clause fails at every edge); the
contrast between doubling and orienting is exactly what \S{}10.6 is about.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A primitive $\mathbb{N}$-matrix: some power is entrywise positive]
\lean{Matrix.IsPrimitive}
\label{Matrix.IsPrimitive}
\leanok
For the adjacency matrix this says: however you pick a starting and
finishing vertex, there is a directed walk of some \emph{common} length $k$ between them.
Corollary 10.7 characterises when a tournament's matrix is primitive --- exactly when
the tournament is diconnected with $\nu \ge 4$.  Primitivity is what licenses
Perron--Frobenius, which gives the convergence of the iterated score vectors
$s_{i} = A^{i}J$ used to rank the players.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits).  Stated for \texttt{Matrix n n $\mathbb{N}$}
rather than the book's \emph{real} matrices, since the only instance needed is the
adjacency matrix; $0 < (R ^ k) i j$ is then the entrywise positivity $R^{k} > 0$.  Note
Mathlib's \texttt{Matrix} order is not entrywise by default, which is why the positivity is
spelled pointwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The de Bruijn digraph $D_n$: vertices are $(n-1)$-bit strings, arcs are left-shifts]
\lean{deBruijnDigraph}
\label{deBruijnDigraph}
\leanok
A vertex is a window of $n-1$ bits; following an arc shifts the window
one place, dropping the leading bit and appending a new one.  Each arc therefore
corresponds to an $n$-bit string --- its label --- and a directed Euler tour reads off
every $n$-bit string exactly once, giving a cyclic binary sequence of length $2^{n}$ in
which all $2^{n}$ windows are distinct.

\emph{The application (\S{}10.5).}  A rotating drum's surface is divided into $2^{n}$
insulating or conducting sections, read by $k$ consecutive contacts.  *First note
that $k$ contacts yield a $k$-digit binary number, and there are $2^{k}$ such numbers.
Therefore, if all $2^{n}$ positions are to give different readings, we must have
$2^{k} \ge 2^{n}$, that is, $k \ge n$* --- and the de Bruijn sequence shows $n$ contacts
suffice.  For $n = 4$ the tour of figure 10.10 gives $0000111100101101$.  Due to
Good (1946).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib and the Archive (0 hits).  A vertex is a
function \texttt{Fin (n-1) $\to$ Bool} rather than a list, so the shift condition is indexed:
\texttt{p ⟨i+1, \_⟩ = q i} for every $i$ with $i + 1 < n - 1$, which is the book's
$1 \le i \le n-2$ in 0-indexed form.  The last coordinate of $q$ is unconstrained, giving
the two out-arcs.  $D_n$ has \textbf{loops} (the all-zeros and all-ones vertices) but no
parallel arcs --- so it is not strict, which is fine, as no \S{}10.5 statement needs
strictness.  Arc labels are not modelled: the label is recoverable from the arc, and
\texttt{exists\_deBruijn\_sequence} states the conclusion about the sequence directly.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[card\_orientations]
\lean{card_orientations}
\label{card_orientations}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsOrientationOf}
An orientation is a choice, independently for each edge, of one of its
two directions; with $\varepsilon$ edges and two choices each the product rule gives $2^\varepsilon$.
These are \emph{labelled} objects: two orientations differing only by a symmetry of $G$
still count separately.

Step 1 is the whole exercise and the \texttt{Sym2} bookkeeping is the
only fiddly part --- the natural first move is to prove a helper turning
\texttt{IsOrientationOf} into "for each edge, exactly one of the two directions".
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[sum\_indegree\_eq\_arcCount]
\lean{sum_indegree_eq_arcCount}
\label{sum_indegree_eq_arcCount}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.arcCount, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree}
The directed handshaking lemma.  Every arc has exactly one head, so
summing indegrees counts each arc once; likewise every arc has one tail.  Contrast
the undirected version (theorem 1.1), where the sum of degrees is $2\varepsilon$: there each
edge is counted twice, once from each end, whereas here the head-count and
tail-count are kept separate and each totals $\varepsilon$.

Stated as a conjunction because the book states both equalities
at once; nothing forces them to share a proof, but step 4 notes they should.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_indegree\_zero\_of\_acyclic]
\lean{exists_indegree_zero_of_acyclic}
\label{exists_indegree_zero_of_acyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
If every vertex had an incoming arc one could walk backwards for ever;
finiteness forces a repeat, and the portion between the two visits is a directed
cycle.  So an acyclic digraph always has a "source" with nothing pointing into it ---
the base of the topological-ordering induction in part (b).

\texttt{[Nonempty V]} is load-bearing: on an empty carrier there is no
$v$ to produce, while \texttt{hacyc} holds vacuously.  Note \texttt{hacyc} also rules out loops,
since a loop is a directed cycle of length $1$ under \texttt{IsDirectedCycle}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_topological\_ordering]
\lean{exists_topological_ordering}
\label{exists_topological_ordering}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.toQuiver}
A \textbf{topological ordering}: line the vertices up so every arrow points
forwards.  Greedy construction via part (a) --- take a source, delete it, repeat.
These are the standard tool for scheduling tasks with prerequisites, and \S{}10.7 uses
the version for the \emph{condensation} of a tournament to order its dicomponents in a
way that preserves dominance.

The book's "every arc with head $v_{i}$ has its tail among the
earlier vertices" is contraposed into the equivalent and more usable
\texttt{D.Adj u v $\to$ f u < f v}.  Note no \texttt{[Nonempty V]} is needed here, unlike part (a) ---
the empty case is the induction's base.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[converse\_converse]
\lean{converse_converse}
\label{converse_converse}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.converse}
Reversing every arrow twice returns each to its original direction, so
the converse is an involution.  That is what makes it a genuine duality: any
statement proved for all digraphs yields its mirror image for free, with in- and
outdegrees and the direction of reachability exchanged --- as parts (ii), (iii) and
(b) then exploit.

The shortest item in the file; a good first fill to shake out the
\texttt{Digraph} extensionality API.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[converse\_indegree]
\lean{converse_indegree}
\label{converse_indegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.converse, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree}
An arc pointing into $v$ in $D$ points out of $v$ in the converse, and
vice versa.  This is the workhorse of the duality: exercise 10.1.5(b) uses it to
turn "acyclic $\Longrightarrow$ $\delta^{-} = 0$" into "acyclic $\Longrightarrow$ $\delta^{+} = 0$" without repeating the
argument.

The \texttt{open scoped Classical in} on this declaration supplies
decidability for \texttt{D.converse.Adj}; step 3 is where that shows up.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[converse\_reachable]
\lean{converse_reachable}
\label{converse_reachable}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Reachable, Digraph.converse}
A directed path from $u$ to $v$ in the converse is exactly a directed
path from $v$ to $u$ in $D$, read backwards.  A useful consequence: diconnection is
\emph{self-dual} --- $D$ is diconnected exactly when $\breve{D}$ is --- since diconnection demands
reachability both ways.

This is the one place where defining \texttt{Reachable} as
\texttt{ReflTransGen} rather than via \texttt{Quiver.Path} pays off directly: no \texttt{Quiver} instance
is in play, so $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} appear in the same statement without
ambiguity.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_outdegree\_zero\_of\_acyclic]
\lean{exists_outdegree_zero_of_acyclic}
\label{exists_outdegree_zero_of_acyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
An acyclic digraph has both a "source" (nothing in) and a "sink"
(nothing out), which is what lets topological ordering be built from either end.
The point of the exercise is methodological: the converse converts one statement
into its dual with no new argument.

Step 1 needs a \texttt{Quiver.Path} reversal for \texttt{D.converse} versus
$D$; since \texttt{toQuiver} is not an instance, both quivers must be named explicitly.
Worth extracting as a standalone lemma, as \texttt{converse\_reachable} is the same fact one
level down.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_directedPath\_length\_ge\_maxMinDegree]
\lean{exists_directedPath_length_ge_maxMinDegree}
\label{exists_directedPath_length_ge_maxMinDegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsStrict, Digraph.minIndegree, Digraph.minOutdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
The directed analogue of exercise 1.6.3.  Strictness is what makes the
counting work: it guarantees the out-neighbours are $\delta^{+}$ genuinely distinct
vertices.

\textbf{!} Step 5 is easy to get wrong.  The statement asks for \textbf{one}
path of length \texttt{$\ge$ max\{$\delta^{-}$, $\delta^{+}$\}}, not one path per bound; since \texttt{max} is one of the
two, produce the two paths and pick the longer.  \texttt{minIndegree}/\texttt{minOutdegree} are
$\bigsqcap$ over $\mathbb{N}$, so \texttt{[Nonempty V]} is needed to keep them from collapsing to $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_directedCycle\_length\_ge]
\lean{exists_directedCycle_length_ge}
\label{exists_directedCycle_length_ge}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.IsStrict, Digraph.minIndegree, Digraph.minOutdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
Sharpens exercise 10.1.6 from paths to cycles, exactly as exercise
1.7.3 sharpens 1.6.3 undirected.  It is consumed inside Ghouila-Houri's theorem
10.4, which opens by noting $l > \nu/2$ for the longest directed cycle --- that is this
exercise with $k \ge \nu/2$.

$hk : 0 < k$ is load-bearing: with $k = 0$ the conclusion would
demand a directed cycle of length $\ge 1$ in a digraph that may have no cycle at all.
\texttt{hdeg} pins \texttt{max $\delta^{-}$ $\delta^{+}$} to $k$ as an equality, matching the book.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[adjMatrix\_pow\_apply\_eq\_card\_directedWalk]
\lean{adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_directedWalk}
\label{adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_directedWalk}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.adjMatrix, Digraph.toQuiver}
The $(i,j)$ entry of $A$ counts arcs, i.e. walks of length one; matrix
multiplication sums over an intermediate vertex, and every walk of length $k$
decomposes uniquely as a shorter walk plus a final arc.  This is the directed
counterpart of exercise 1.6.2, and it is what makes \S{}10.7's ranking work: the
$i$-th level score vector is $A^{i}J$, counting directed walks of length $i$ out of
each player.  Theorem 10.7 consumes it directly.

\textbf{!} Restated for a $0/1$ matrix, \texttt{Digraph} having no arc
multiplicities; for the strict digraphs of \S{}10.7 this is no loss.  The right-hand
side is \texttt{Nat.card} of a subtype of \texttt{Quiver.Path}, which is finite because the length
is pinned --- but that finiteness may need to be supplied for \texttt{Nat.card} to behave.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[condensation\_acyclic]
\lean{condensation_acyclic}
\label{condensation_acyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.condensation, Digraph.toQuiver}
A directed cycle among dicomponents would merge them into one, so
contracting always produces an acyclic digraph --- which by exercise 10.1.3(b) can be
topologically ordered.  \S{}10.7 uses exactly this to rank the dicomponents of a
non-diconnected tournament in a dominance-preserving order, and exercise 10.2.1 uses
it on tournaments.

Step 3 is where \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}'s defining
property is consumed; the useful form is "same component $\leftrightarrow$ mutually reachable",
which should be extracted first.  Note the statement quantifies over all base points
$c$, since \texttt{IsDirectedCycle} is stated for closed paths at a given vertex.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_balanced\_orientation]
\lean{exists_balanced_orientation}
\label{exists_balanced_orientation}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsOrientationOf, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree}
Every graph can be made one-way in a \emph{balanced} way, with the traffic
into and out of each junction differing by at most one.  Contrast exercise 10.6.1,
which shows the stronger set-wise balance --- $||(S, \bar{S})| - |(\bar{S}, S)|| \le 1$ for every
vertex \emph{set} $S$ --- is \textbf{not} always achievable, the Petersen graph being a
counterexample.

The conclusion is stated as two $\mathbb{Z}$ inequalities rather than
$|\cdot| \le 1$, avoiding \texttt{Int.natAbs} juggling.  The \texttt{open scoped Classical in} supplies
decidability of the existentially-bound \texttt{D.Adj}; the outline's
\texttt{$\exists$ \_ : DecidableRel D.Adj} does not register as an instance inside the body, which
is why it was replaced.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[roy\_gallai\_directed\_path]
\lean{roy_gallai_directed_path}
\label{roy_gallai_directed_path}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.toQuiver}
(Roy, 1967; Gallai, 1968).  *A digraph $D$ contains a directed
path of length $\chi - 1$*, where $\chi$ is the chromatic number of the underlying
graph.

Striking because, as figure 10.3 shows, there is otherwise *no close
relationship between the lengths of paths and directed paths in a digraph* --- yet the
chromatic number of the underlying graph controls the latter exactly.  The remark
following shows the bound is best possible.

$k - 1$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction, harmless as the goal is a lower bound.
$hk$ pins $\chi$ of \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive} --- the underlying graph --- to $k$ in $\mathbb{N}\infty$.
Step 4 is the mathematical core; steps 1 and 2 are both "choose a maximum/minimum in
a finite nonempty family" and should share a helper.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_orientation\_longest\_directedPath\_le]
\lean{exists_orientation_longest_directedPath_le}
\label{exists_orientation_longest_directedPath_le}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, Digraph.toQuiver}
Orient every edge from the lower colour class to the higher.  Along a
directed path the colour index strictly increases, so the path has at most $\chi$
vertices.  Combined with theorem 10.1 this shows $\chi - 1$ is exactly the right
bound.  Note the orientation is automatically acyclic, the colour index being a
topological ordering --- so this also witnesses exercise 10.1.3(b) in reverse.

Stated with an arbitrary $k$-colouring rather than an optimal
one, which is the usable form: exercise 10.2.6(a) instantiates it at $k = \Delta + 1$
via corollary 8.1.2, not at $k = \chi$.  Step 4's injectivity is a cleaner invariant
to carry than the book's "no two vertices share a colour".
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[redei\_directed\_hamilton\_path]
\lean{redei_directed_hamilton_path}
\label{redei_directed_hamilton_path}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.toQuiver}
(R\'edei, 1934).  *Every tournament has a directed Hamilton
path.*

B\&M define the term just above: *A directed Hamilton path of $D$ is a directed path
that includes every vertex of $D$.*

In any round-robin competition the players can be lined up so that
each beat the next.  The book cautions in \S{}10.7 that this does \emph{not} give a sensible
ranking, since a tournament generally has many directed Hamilton paths --- the
six-player example has $(3,1,2,4,5,6)$, $(1,2,4,5,6,3)$, $(1,4,6,3,2,5)$ and others,
declaring different winners.  That is what motivates the eigenvector method.

"Includes every vertex" is \texttt{$\forall$ w, w $\in$ p.vertices} rather than a
cardinality claim, which is what step 3 delivers most directly.  Exercise 10.2.3
gives an independent route not passing through theorem 10.1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_lovasz\_semikernel]
\lean{chvatal_lovasz_semikernel}
\label{chvatal_lovasz_semikernel}
\leanok
(Chv\'atal and Lov\'asz, 1974).  *A loopless digraph $D$ has an
independent set $S$ such that each vertex of $D$ not in $S$ is reachable from a
vertex in $S$ by a directed path of length at most two.*

Such a set is called a \textbf{semi-kernel}.  The independence requirement
is what makes it non-trivial --- one wants mutually non-adjacent "dominators" from
which everything else is within two steps.  Corollary 10.2 is the tournament case,
where independence forces $|S| = 1$.

The $u = v$ disjunct in the goal covers the reflexive case and is
not in the book, which says "each vertex \emph{not in} $S$"; it is harmless and makes the
statement easier to instantiate.  \texttt{hloop : Irreflexive D.Adj} is B\&M's "loopless".
\texttt{IsIndepSet} is taken in \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive}, matching "independent set" for the
underlying graph.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tournament\_exists\_king]
\lean{tournament_exists_king}
\label{tournament_exists_king}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsTournament}
*A tournament contains a vertex from which every other
vertex is reachable by a directed path of length at most two.*

Such a vertex is called a \textbf{king}: a player who, for every other
player $v$, either beat $v$ directly or beat someone who beat $v$.  Exercise 10.2.4
gives a direct proof --- take a vertex of maximum outdegree --- which is dropped from
this file as a second proof of the same statement.  Note a king need not have won
the most games, and a tournament may have several kings.

\texttt{[Nonempty V]} is load-bearing for step 3; without it $S = \emptyset$ is
a legitimate semi-kernel and no $u$ exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tournament\_diconnected\_or\_reorient\_one]
\lean{tournament_diconnected_or_reorient_one}
\label{tournament_diconnected_or_reorient_one}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsTournament}
Tournaments are never far from diconnected: a single reversed result
suffices to make every player reachable from every other.  Step 3 is the tournament
speciality --- in a general digraph the dicomponents form only a partial order, and
one reversal would not do.

The reorientation is written inline as an $if$-cascade on \texttt{Adj}
rather than via a helper: $(x,y)$ is removed, $(y,x)$ added, everything else kept.
Note the \texttt{if (u = y $\land$ v = x) then True} branch must come \emph{after} the $(x,y)$ branch,
which it does.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isUnilateral\_iff\_exists\_spanning\_directedWalk]
\lean{isUnilateral_iff_exists_spanning_directedWalk}
\label{isUnilateral_iff_exists_spanning_directedWalk}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsUnilateral, Digraph.toQuiver}
\emph{.  }$D$ is unilateral if and only if $D$ has a spanning
directed walk.*

Unilateral means any two vertices are comparable --- you can get from
one to the other, though perhaps only one way round.  It sits strictly between
"connected" and "diconnected".

\textbf{!} The book genuinely means \emph{walk}, not path: revisiting vertices
is essential, since a spanning directed \textbf{path} would be a Hamilton path and is a
far stronger requirement.  The Lean statement accordingly asks only for a
\texttt{Quiver.Path} (= directed walk) whose \texttt{vertices} cover $V$, with \textbf{no} \texttt{Nodup}
condition --- do not be tempted to add \texttt{IsDirectedPath}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tournament\_maximal\_directedPath\_insert]
\lean{tournament_maximal_directedPath_insert}
\label{tournament_maximal_directedPath_insert}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsTournament}
*Let $P = (v_{1}, \dots, v_k)$ be a maximal directed path in a
tournament $D$.  Suppose $P$ is not a directed Hamilton path and let $v$ be any
vertex not on $P$.  Then for some $i$, both $(v_{i}, v)$ and $(v, v_{i+1})$ are arcs
of $D$.*

Because $D$ is a tournament, $v$ is joined to every vertex of $P$ in
one direction or the other; maximality forces $v_{1} \to v$ at the start and
$v \to v_k$ at the end, so travelling along $P$ the direction must switch somewhere.
Part (b) --- dropped here, being a re-derivation of corollary 10.1 --- inserts $v$ at
that point to get a longer directed path and repeats until it spans.

The path is presented as a \texttt{List V} with \texttt{IsChain D.Adj} rather
than as a \texttt{Quiver.Path}, since the statement indexes into it ($l[i]$, $l[i+1]$) and
lists index far more comfortably.  \texttt{[Inhabited V]} supports \texttt{head!}/\texttt{getLast!} in
\texttt{hmax}; \texttt{hne : l $\ne$ []} keeps those meaningful.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_komlos\_monotone\_directedPath]
\lean{chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath}
\label{chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath}
\leanok
\emph{ (Chv\'atal and Koml\'os).  }Let $D$ be a digraph with
$\chi > mn$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on $V$.  Then $D$ has either a
directed path $(u_{0}, \dots, u_m)$ with $f(u_{0}) \le f(u_{1}) \le \dots \le f(u_m)$, or a directed path
$(v_{0}, \dots, v_n)$ with $f(v_{0}) > f(v_{1}) > \dots > f(v_n)$.*

Theorem 10.1 says a high chromatic number forces a long directed path;
this refines it by controlling how $f$ behaves along that path.  A large enough
chromatic number forces a \emph{monotone} directed path --- weakly increasing of length
$m$, or strictly decreasing of length $n$.  Part (b) reads off Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres.

Paths are \texttt{List V} with two \texttt{IsChain}s --- one for adjacency, one
for the $f$-comparison --- plus \texttt{Nodup}, rather than \texttt{Quiver.Path}s, so that the
monotonicity condition can be stated alongside.  Note the asymmetry $\le$ versus $>$
is the book's and is essential: with two weak orders step 3 would fail on an arc
where $f u = f w$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[erdos\_szekeres\_of\_chvatal\_komlos]
\lean{erdos_szekeres_of_chvatal_komlos}
\label{erdos_szekeres_of_chvatal_komlos}
\leanok
\emph{ (Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres).  }Deduce that any sequence of
$mn + 1$ distinct integers contains either an increasing subsequence of $m$ terms
or a decreasing subsequence of $n$ terms.*

The classical Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres theorem, obtained as a special case of a
statement about digraphs --- a good illustration of the chapter's theme that
chromatic number controls directed-path structure.

\textbf{!} Restated: Mathlib's \texttt{Archive} version is not importable, so
the statement is spelled out here and derived from (a) as the book intends.  $g$ is
$\mathbb{Z}$-valued (the book's "integers") while part (a) needs $\mathbb{R}$, hence the cast in step
2.  \texttt{hN : m * n < N} is the book's "$mn + 1$ terms", generalised to any longer
sequence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_orientation\_directedPath\_le\_maxDegree]
\lean{exists_orientation_directedPath_le_maxDegree}
\label{exists_orientation_directedPath_le_maxDegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, Digraph.toQuiver}
*Using theorem 10.1 and corollary 8.1.2, show that $G$
has an orientation in which each directed path is of length at most $\Delta$.*

Chaining two results already available: $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ bounds the palette,
and the colour-increasing orientation turns a palette bound into a path bound.  Part
(b) of the exercise --- dropped here, being the same statement --- asks for a
constructive proof avoiding the chromatic detour.

\textbf{!} This rides chapter 8's corollary 8.1.2, which is out of
chapter; step 1 is therefore an import from
\texttt{TCSlib/GraphTheory/VertexColourings.lean} (\texttt{chromaticNumber\_le\_maxDegree\_add\_one})
rather than something proved here.  Note the shape of step 2: this is exactly why
the theorem-10.1 remark was stated for an arbitrary $k$-colouring rather than an
optimal one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[moon\_vertex\_pancyclic]
\lean{moon_vertex_pancyclic}
\label{moon_vertex_pancyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.toQuiver}
(Moon, 1966).  *Each vertex of a diconnected tournament $D$
with $\nu \ge 3$ is contained in a directed $k$-cycle, $3 \le k \le \nu$.*

A digraph with this property is \textbf{vertex-pancyclic}: every vertex lies
on cycles of \emph{every} possible length.  Taking $k = \nu$, every diconnected tournament
has a directed Hamilton cycle --- first proved by Camion (1959).  Theorem 10.7
consumes the full strength, needing cycles of several specific lengths through a
given vertex.

The cycle is based at $u$ (\texttt{p : Path u u}), which is how "$u$ is
contained in" is expressed.  \textbf{!} The book's final splice $(v_{0}, v, w, v_{2}, \dots, v_n)$
silently assumes $v$ follows $v_{0}$ and $w$ precedes $v_{2}$; check the index bookkeeping
against $n \ge 3$ before trusting it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ghouila\_houri\_directed\_hamilton\_cycle]
\lean{ghouila_houri_directed_hamilton_cycle}
\label{ghouila_houri_directed_hamilton_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.IsStrict, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
(a special case of Ghouila-Houri, 1960).  *If $D$ is strict and
\texttt{min\{$\delta^{-}$, $\delta^{+}$\} $\ge$ $\nu$/2 > 1}, then $D$ contains a directed Hamilton cycle.*

The directed extension of Dirac's theorem 4.3 --- a large minimum degree,
now in \emph{both} directions, forces a spanning cycle.  Exercise 10.3.1 recovers Dirac
from it by orienting a graph suitably.

\texttt{hdeg} states $\nu \le 2 d^{-}(v)$ and $\nu \le 2 d^{+}(v)$ rather than
\texttt{min\{$\delta^{-}$,$\delta^{+}$\} $\ge$ $\nu$/2}, avoiding division; $hv : 2 < \nu$ is the book's $\nu/2 > 1$.  The
result is only a \emph{special case} of Ghouila-Houri's theorem, as B\&M note.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff]
\lean{exists_directedEulerTour_iff}
\label{exists_directedEulerTour_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedEulerTour, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
*$D$ contains a directed Euler tour if and only if $D$ is
connected and $d^{+}(v) = d^{-}(v)$ for all $v \in V$.*

The directed analogue of Euler's theorem 4.1.  Every visit uses one
arrow in and one out, so the two counts must balance.  \emph{Why it is built early:}
\S{}10.5 depends on it --- the de Bruijn digraph $D_n$ is connected with every indegree
and outdegree $2$, so it has a directed Euler tour, and that tour is exactly the
binary sequence for the computer drum.

Connectivity is asked of \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive}, the underlying
graph, matching B\&M's "$D$ is connected" (a property of the underlying graph, per
\S{}10.1).

\textbf{+} \textbf{Statement repaired --- connectivity moved from the right-hand side into a
hypothesis.}  As previously written, \texttt{($\exists$ Euler tour) $\leftrightarrow$ (Connected $\land$ balanced)}, the
$\leftrightarrow$ was \textbf{false}, for two compounding reasons.

\emph{Counterexample 1.}  Let $D$ have no arcs and \texttt{card V $\ge$ 2}.  Then \texttt{Quiver.Path.nil} at
any $u$ satisfies \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour} --- its arc list is $[]$ (so \texttt{Nodup}), and the
exhaustiveness clause \texttt{$\forall$ a b, D.Adj a b $\to$ \dots} is vacuous --- so the left side holds,
while the right side fails because $D$ is disconnected.

\emph{Counterexample 2.}  Adding arcs does not rescue it: take one directed cycle plus an
isolated vertex.  A tour of the cycle exhausts every arc, so the left side holds, but
the underlying graph is still disconnected.

So no strengthening of the left side repairs this; connectivity has to be assumed, not
concluded.  With \texttt{hconn} a hypothesis the equivalence is the honest directed Euler
theorem, and it now matches the shape of this library's undirected
\texttt{euler\_tour\_iff\_no\_odd\_degree} in \texttt{EulerHamilton.lean}.

\textbf{!} Note that unlike the undirected statement, \textbf{no arc-nonemptiness hypothesis is
needed}: \texttt{hconn} already forces the arc-free case to be the one-vertex graph, where
\texttt{nil} is an Euler tour and the balance condition holds vacuously, so the $\leftrightarrow$ is true
there.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_arcDisjoint\_directedPaths]
\lean{exists_arcDisjoint_directedPaths}
\label{exists_arcDisjoint_directedPaths}
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.arcsOf, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
*Let $D$ be a digraph such that (i)
$d^{+}(x) - d^{-}(x) = l = d^{-}(y) - d^{+}(y)$ and (ii) $d^{+}(v) = d^{-}(v)$ for
$v \in V \ {x, y}$.  Show, using exercise 10.3.2, that there exist $l$ arc-disjoint
directed $(x, y)$-paths in $D$.*

The degree conditions say $x$ has an excess of $l$ outgoing arcs, $y$
an excess of $l$ incoming ones, and everything else is balanced --- so $l$ units of
"flow" must run from $x$ to $y$.  A small precursor of the max-flow min-cut
machinery of chapter 11.

\textbf{!} Two obstructions to the intended route, both recorded rather
than resolved.  (i) \texttt{Digraph} admits \textbf{no parallel arcs}, so step 1's "$l$ copies of
$(y,x)$" is not expressible on $D$; the construction has to move to
\texttt{Digraph (V $\oplus$ Fin l)}, routing each extra arc through its own new vertex.  The
\emph{statement} stays on $D$ and is well-typed.  (ii) The conclusion mentions \texttt{arcsOf},
which currently has a \texttt{sorry} body, so the arc-disjointness clause is presently
meaningless --- see that definition.  Degrees are compared in $\mathbb{Z}$ to let $hx$, $hy$
state genuine differences without $\mathbb{N}$-truncation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_directed\_odd\_cycle]
\lean{exists_directed_odd_cycle}
\label{exists_directed_odd_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.toQuiver}
\emph{.  }A diconnected digraph which contains an odd cycle also
contains a directed odd cycle.*

The hypothesis gives an odd cycle in the \emph{underlying} graph, whose arcs
may point every which way; the conclusion upgrades it to a genuinely directed odd
cycle.  Diconnection is essential --- without it the parity argument cannot be
propagated across the whole digraph, and the statement is false.

The undirected cycle enters as a \texttt{Walk} in
\texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive} with \texttt{IsCycle} and \texttt{Odd length}; the directed conclusion is
a \texttt{Quiver.Path}.  Step 2's "decompose a closed walk into directed cycles" has no
Mathlib counterpart for \texttt{Quiver.Path} and will have to be built.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one]
\lean{diconnected_iff_isKArcConnected_one}
\label{diconnected_iff_isKArcConnected_one}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsKArcConnected}
*A nontrivial digraph is diconnected if and only if it is
1-arc-connected.*

Diconnection is the $k = 1$ case of arc-connectivity, exactly as
connection is the $k = 1$ case of edge-connectivity in \S{}3.1.

\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} is the book's "nontrivial digraph" and is
load-bearing: on a one-vertex carrier there is no nonempty proper $S$, so
\texttt{IsKArcConnected 1} is vacuously true while \texttt{Diconnected} --- which is also true there
--- would make the $\leftrightarrow$ hold only by accident.  More importantly, its absence is what
breaks \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} below.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff]
\lean{associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff}
\label{associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsKArcConnected, SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph, edgeConnectivity}
*$D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected if and only if $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.*

The associated digraph faithfully preserves connectivity, so the
directed notion generalises the undirected one.  Contrast \S{}10.6, where the question
is which \emph{orientations} --- not the doubling --- preserve it; there the answer is much
more delicate (Robbins, Nash-Williams).

"$G$ is $k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G},
per \S{}3.1.  Step 2 needs that a minimal edge cut is $[S, S^{c}]$ for a component $S$,
which is the same fact the local \texttt{IsEdgeCut} docstring notes when reconciling the
book's shape-based definition with the deletion-based one used here.

\textbf{+} \textbf{Statement repaired --- \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} added.}  The $\leftrightarrow$ was \textbf{false on a
one-vertex carrier}.  Take \texttt{card V = 1}, so $G = \bot$, and $k = 1$.  \emph{Left side:} there
is no nonempty proper \texttt{S : Finset V}, so \texttt{IsKArcConnected 1} holds vacuously.  *Right
side:* $\bot$ on one vertex is \texttt{Connected}, so nothing disconnects it, $G$ has no edge cut
at all, and \texttt{edgeConnectivity G = 0}; the claim $1 \le 0$ fails.

\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} excludes exactly that carrier and is the hypothesis the book's
"nontrivial digraph" convention supplies implicitly (compare
\texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one} above, which already carries it).  \textbf{!} Both Menger
statements in \texttt{Networks.lean} consume this lemma, so their hypotheses must be checked
against the added \texttt{Nontrivial} when they are proved.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[deBruijnDigraph\_indegree\_eq\_two]
\lean{deBruijnDigraph_indegree_eq_two}
\label{deBruijnDigraph_indegree_eq_two}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, deBruijnDigraph}
A vertex is a window of $n-1$ bits.  Its out-neighbours drop the
leading bit and append a new one --- two choices; its in-neighbours drop the trailing
bit and prepend a new one --- again two.  This is the balance condition exercise
10.3.2 needs, and is why $D_n$ has a directed Euler tour.

$hn : 2 \le n$ is load-bearing in step 3: for $n = 1$ the carrier
\texttt{Fin 0 $\to$ Bool} is a singleton and the free coordinate does not exist, so the two
neighbours coincide and the degree is $1$, not $2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[deBruijnDigraph\_connected]
\lean{deBruijnDigraph_connected}
\label{deBruijnDigraph_connected}
\leanok
\uses{deBruijnDigraph}
From any binary string one can reach any other by shifting in the
target's bits one at a time; after $n - 1$ shifts the window contains exactly the
target.  Together with the degree balance above, this is the second half of the
Euler-tour criterion of exercise 10.3.2.

The explicit walk of step 1 is the whole content; a slick
argument is unlikely to be shorter than just writing the $n - 1$ intermediate
vertices down as a function of the step index.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[deBruijnDigraph\_exists\_directedEulerTour]
\lean{deBruijnDigraph_exists_directedEulerTour}
\label{deBruijnDigraph_exists_directedEulerTour}
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedEulerTour, Digraph.toQuiver, deBruijnDigraph}
Each arc carries an $n$-bit label and the tour uses every arc exactly
once, so reading off the first digit of each label in order produces a cyclic binary
sequence of length $2^{n}$ in which all $2^{n}$ windows of length $n$ are distinct.

\emph{The application.}  Divide a rotating drum's surface into $2^{n}$ sections according to
that sequence; then $n$ consecutive contacts read a different $n$-bit number at each
of the $2^{n}$ positions, so all positions are distinguishable --- and $n$ is optimal,
since $k$ contacts give only $2^{k}$ readings.  For $n = 4$ the book's tour gives
$0000111100101101$.  Due to Good (1946).

\textbf{!} This is a three-line consequence of its two inputs, but it
inherits both defects of \texttt{exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff}: that theorem is currently
false as stated, and \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour} is defined through the \texttt{sorry}-bodied
\texttt{arcsOf}.  Until those are repaired this statement is not the intended one.  Note
also that the \emph{labels} are not modelled --- the conclusion asserts a tour exists, and
turning it into the binary sequence is left to \texttt{exists\_deBruijn\_sequence}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[robbins\_orientation]
\lean{robbins_orientation}
\label{robbins_orientation}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, edgeConnectivity}
(Robbins, 1939).  *If $G$ is 2-edge-connected, then $G$ has a
diconnected orientation.*

How to make a road system one-way so traffic can still flow
everywhere.  A graph with a cut edge clearly cannot manage it --- whichever way that
edge is directed, one side becomes unreachable --- and Robbins showed
2-edge-connectivity is not merely necessary but sufficient.  Intuitively, each new
vertex is given both a way in and a way out.

\textbf{!} Step 2 rides chapter 3's exercise 3.2.1, which this repo does
not have; budget for it before starting.  \texttt{h2ec : 2 $\le$ edgeConnectivity G} is
"$2$-edge-connected" per \S{}3.1.  Theorem 10.6 is the $k = 1$ case of a different
route to the same conclusion, so neither theorem subsumes the other.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian]
\lean{exists_kArcConnected_orientation_of_eulerian}
\label{exists_kArcConnected_orientation_of_eulerian}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsKArcConnected, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, edgeConnectivity}
*Let $G$ be a $2k$-edge-connected graph with an Euler trail.
Then $G$ has a $k$-arc-connected orientation.*

The easy special case of a theorem of Nash-Williams (1960), that
\emph{every} $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected orientation; the general
proof is difficult.  Robbins' theorem 10.5 is the case $k = 1$ --- proved there by a
quite different, ear-decomposition route.

\textbf{!} Step 4's $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ is stated as \texttt{2 * count + 1 $\ge$ m} to keep $\mathbb{N}$
division out.  Step 2 is where an Euler \emph{trail} rather than a tour matters: an open
trail is what allows the discrepancy of one, and a closed tour would give equality.
Note \texttt{t : G.Walk u v} with $u$, $v$ unconstrained, so both cases are covered.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tournament\_adjMatrix\_pow\_pos]
\lean{tournament_adjMatrix_pow_pos}
\label{tournament_adjMatrix_pow_pos}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.adjMatrix, Digraph.dirDiameter}
*Let $D$ be a diconnected tournament with $\nu \ge 5$, and let $A$
be the adjacency matrix of $D$.  Then $A^{d+3} > 0$ (every entry positive), where
$d$ is the directed diameter of $D$.*

\emph{Why it matters (\S{}10.7).}  The $i$-th level score vector of a
tournament is $s_{i} = A^{i}J$, each player's score being the sum of the scores of those
they beat.  Primitivity of $A$ is what lets Perron--Frobenius guarantee these vectors
converge to a positive eigenvector, giving a well-defined ranking.

\textbf{!} The arithmetic $d - d_{ij} + 3$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction but never
truncates, since $d_{ij} \le d$; still, establish that inequality before the case split
rather than relying on it implicitly.  $\nu \ge 5$ is load-bearing in step 4 only.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tournament\_adjMatrix\_isPrimitive\_iff]
\lean{tournament_adjMatrix_isPrimitive_iff}
\label{tournament_adjMatrix_isPrimitive_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.adjMatrix, Matrix.IsPrimitive}
*The adjacency matrix $A$ of a tournament $D$ is primitive
if and only if $D$ is diconnected and $\nu \ge 4$.*

\emph{The ranking method (\S{}10.7).}  When $A$ is primitive, Perron--Frobenius
gives a largest real eigenvalue $r$ with \texttt{lim\_i (A/r)$^{i}$ J = s}, a positive
eigenvector; the normalised $\bar{s}$ measures relative strengths.  For the book's
six-player example $r \approx 2.232$ and $\bar{s} \approx (.238, .164, .231, .113, .150, .104)$,
ranking the players $1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6$.  Non-diconnected tournaments are handled by
ranking within dicomponents and then ordering the dicomponents by dominance
(exercises 10.1.9 and 10.1.3(b)).  Due to Wei (1952) and Kendall (1955).

\textbf{!} Steps 2 and 4 are the awkward ones: B\&M discharge them by
pointing at a figure the source omits, so the two small tournaments have to be
identified and checked from scratch.  Everything else follows from theorem 10.7 and
exercise 10.1.8.
\end{theorem}
